# Where State Lives {#sec-containers}

Statefulness is fine. Undeclared statefulness is what bites. Picking a
container is picking where identity, validation, and lifetime live, and
the runtime has already limited the menu. You do not invent a third
physics. You choose a value or a handle, and you say so in the type.

## Four questions

Ask them in order.

1. **Does anyone need to observe mutation of the same object?** An open
   connection, a token that refreshes, a cache, a progress meter, a
   conversation. Yes means a {{< glossary "reference owner" >}}: an
   environment, an R6 object, an external pointer, or an S7 class that
   has deliberately chosen environment physics. No means a value. Lists,
   S3 objects, and ordinary S7 objects are values. Copy-on-modify is the
   physics, whether you think about it or not.

2. **Is this a domain fact or a process capability?** Config, enums,
   colors, response schemas, and parsed documents are facts. They want
   to be values, because you want to compare them, print them, and put
   them in tests. "Talk to this API," "hold this socket," "retry with
   backoff" are capabilities. They want a handle that *owns* or
   *receives* values.

3. **Who owns the lifetime?** Process-wide defaults belong in a small
   package environment or in `options()`, documented, and treated as
   defaults rather than as the real API. Per session, per test, per
   request: construct the value or the handle and pass it. Hidden `<<-`
   into a parent the caller cannot name is how a helper becomes a seance.

4. **Where do the contracts live?** This is not "S7 or S3 depending on
   how serious you are." Illegal states should be unrepresentable either
   way. The question is whether the contract is a ritual you maintain
   (`new_*`, `validate_*`, `as_*`, `format_*`) or a structure the object
   carries (S7 properties, validators, generics). @sec-types takes that
   fork. It does not weaken question 1.

## A concrete map

The API-shaped version, because it keeps coming up:

| Thing | Container | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api_config`: base URL, timeouts, auth material, enums | S7 or S3 value | A snapshot. Cheap to compare. Easy to build in a test. No identity. |
| `api_client`: request factory, token refresh, rate limit | R6, an environment, or a thin handle around httr2 | Identity matters. The token you refresh is the token the next call must see. |
| Package default config | Locked package environment, or `options()` | Bootstrapping. Override by argument, not by a global write in the hot path. |
| Call-site wiring | Pass the client in | Tests inject fakes. Scripts inject the real handle. |

```text
config   : value     what is true
client   : handle    what can act
functions: take the handle, and take config overrides as values
package environment: defaults and registries only
```

The anti-pattern is one class that is both the config record and the live
session. You then either mutate a thing that prints like a value, or you
copy a thing that was supposed to be a handle and wonder why the refresh
did not stick. The physics will not save you from that confusion. It will
obey whichever choice you accidentally made.

Gary Bernhardt's talk
[Boundaries](https://www.destroyallsoftware.com/talks/boundaries) names the
larger shape: a functional core that decides, an imperative shell that
performs effects. In R the core is values and verbs. The shell is the
handle, the `options()` read at the edge, the handler that decides how a
condition is shown. "Functional core, imperative shell" is not a style
for people who dislike objects. It is a rule for where objects with
identity are allowed to stand.

## Dependency injection without the enterprise voice

Passing the client is dependency injection. You do not need a container
framework. You need an argument.

- **Package environment or options.** Defaults, feature flags, a memoised
  registry, the current printing width. Ambient, documented, easy to
  override in a test by setting the option inside `withr::with_options`
  or by not reading the option when an argument was supplied.
- **Arguments.** Anything that changes the correctness of a call. If a
  test must swap it, it is an argument, or it is a field of a handle that
  was built from an argument.
- **The hybrid that stays sane.** `client <- api_client_new(config = api_config_default())`,
  and `api_config_default()` reads the option once. Callers who care pass
  a config they built themselves. Callers who do not care get the
  default. Nobody reaches through `<<-`.

This is also the answer to "a package environment versus a client that
closes over the config." The package environment is a process-lifetime
default. The client is a value you chose to give identity because it acts.
Functions that quietly call `get_config()` from the package environment
are hard to test and hard to reason about, and they feel convenient for
exactly as long as you have one config. The day you have two --- prod and
sandbox, this tenant and that tenant --- the hidden lookup becomes the
bug.

## Reactivity is the tell

The notebook's guess about reference semantics was right, and it is the
best reason to choose a handle on purpose. If a later step must observe
that *this* object changed --- invalidate a cache, advance a progress
bar, refresh a token that other calls share --- then identity is part of
the feature. Values can imitate this with explicit returns and with
reactive frameworks that diff old and new, and sometimes that imitation
is the point. Shiny's reactive graph is a disciplined version. It is a
lot of machinery to reach for when an environment would have been the
honest model.

The converse tell: if you never observe identity, a reference object is
paying for a capability you do not use, and you are giving up the ability
to treat the thing as a value in tests and in pipes. S7 getters and
setters do not change this. A setter on a value returns a new value. A
setter on a handle mutates. The syntax can be made to look similar. The
addresses will not.

## Superassignment, one last time

`<<-` is the undeclared version of a handle. It can implement the same
patterns, and people do, and the patterns work until the enclosure chain
is not the one they imagined. Lexical scope is a feature when you are
resolving a free variable on purpose. It is a liability when you are
using it as a mutable store you refused to name.

If you want the pattern "scratch space inside a function, value out," do
that with a local environment and return a list or an S7 object. The
environment dies with the call. The value carries the facts. That is the
`ST` pattern from @sec-illusion, performed by hand, and it is a good
pattern. The moment the environment is returned, or stored in the package
environment, you have built a handle. Then name it as a handle and give
it a type, so the next reader does not have to discover the identity by
calling `lobstr::obj_addr`.
